claim: Drosophila females store more fat than males.
source: For example, Drosophila females store more fat than males.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction as an established fact about the sex difference in fat storage.

claim: Loss of Tra in females reduced whole-body fat storage.
source: We show that loss of Tra in females reduced whole-body fat storage, whereas gain of Tra in males augmented fat storage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the abstract and detailed in Figure 1A.

claim: Gain of Tra in males augmented fat storage.
source: We show that loss of Tra in females reduced whole-body fat storage, whereas gain of Tra in males augmented fat storage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the abstract and detailed in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Tra's role in promoting fat storage was largely due to its function in neurons, specifically the Adipokinetic hormone (Akh)-producing cells (APCs).
source: Tra's role in promoting fat storage was largely due to its function in neurons, specifically the Adipokinetic hormone (Akh)-producing cells (APCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that neuron-specific and APC-specific Tra expression affects fat storage, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is a male bias in APC activity.
source: Our analysis of Akh pathway regulation revealed a male bias in APC activity and Akh pathway function, where this sex-biased regulation influenced the sex difference in fat storage by limiting triglyceride accumulation in males.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing higher GFP intensity in male APCs compared to females using the CaLexA system, as shown in Figure 3D-H.

claim: There is a male bias in Akh pathway function.
source: Our analysis of Akh pathway regulation revealed a male bias in APC activity and Akh pathway function, where this sex-biased regulation influenced the sex difference in fat storage by limiting triglyceride accumulation in males.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing higher Akh and AkhR mRNA levels in males (Figure 3A-B) and higher p-Ire1 levels in males (Figure 3I-K).

claim: Sex-biased regulation of the Akh pathway influences the sex difference in fat storage by limiting triglyceride accumulation in males.
source: Our analysis of Akh pathway regulation revealed a male bias in APC activity and Akh pathway function, where this sex-biased regulation influenced the sex difference in fat storage by limiting triglyceride accumulation in males.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that genetic manipulation of the Akh pathway has male-biased effects on fat storage, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Tra loss in females increased Akh pathway activity.
source: Importantly, Tra loss in females increased Akh pathway activity, and genetically manipulating the Akh pathway rescued Tra-dependent effects on fat storage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing higher p-Ire1 levels and Akh mRNA levels in tra mutant females, as shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Genetically manipulating the Akh pathway rescued Tra-dependent effects on fat storage.
source: Importantly, Tra loss in females increased Akh pathway activity, and genetically manipulating the Akh pathway rescued Tra-dependent effects on fat storage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that APC ablation in tra mutant females rescued the decrease in fat storage, as shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: In mammals, females store approximately 10% more body fat than males.
source: In mammals, females store approximately 10% more body fat than males (Jackson et al., 2002; Karastergiou et al., 2012; Womersley and Durnin, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Female insects can store up to four times more fat than males of the same species.
source: Female insects, on the other hand, can store up to four times more fat than males of the same species (Lease and Wolf, 2011) and break down fat more slowly than males when nutrients are scarce (Wat et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Female insects break down fat more slowly than males when nutrients are scarce.
source: Female insects, on the other hand, can store up to four times more fat than males of the same species (Lease and Wolf, 2011) and break down fat more slowly than males when nutrients are scarce (Wat et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Females with reduced fat storage often show lower fecundity.
source: These male-female differences in fat metabolism play a key role in supporting successful reproduction in each sex: females with reduced fat storage often show lower fecundity (Buszczak et al., 2002; Sieber and Spradling, 2015) whereas males with excess fat storage generally show decreased fertility (Grönke et al., 2005; Wat et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Males with excess fat storage generally show decreased fertility.
source: These male-female differences in fat metabolism play a key role in supporting successful reproduction in each sex: females with reduced fat storage often show lower fecundity (Buszczak et al., 2002; Sieber and Spradling, 2015) whereas males with excess fat storage generally show decreased fertility (Grönke et al., 2005; Wat et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly lower in tra1/Df(3L)st-j7 females compared with w1118 control females.
source: In 5-day-old virgin females lacking tra function (tra1/Df(3L)st-j7), we found that whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly lower than in age-matched w1118 control females (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A with statistical significance p<0.0001.

claim: There was no significant difference in fat storage between tra1/Df(3L)st-j7 mutant males and w1118 control males.
source: Because we observed no significant difference in fat storage between tra1/Df(3L)st-j7 mutant males and w1118 control males (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), the sex difference in whole-body triglyceride storage was reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tra's effect on whole-body triglyceride storage was not explained by the absence of ovaries in females lacking Tra function.
source: While previous studies show the ovaries store a small amount of triglyceride (Sieber and Spradling, 2015; Wat et al., 2020), Tra's effect on whole-body triglyceride storage was not explained by the absence of ovaries in females lacking Tra function: whole-body fat storage was still significantly lower in tra1/Df(3L)st-j7 mutant females with excised gonads compared with w1118 control females with excised ovaries (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing gonadless flies.

claim: Whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly higher in da-GAL4>UAS-traF males compared with da-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-traF control males.
source: In 5-day-old da-GAL4>UAS-traF males, whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly higher than in age-matched da-GAL4>+ or +>UAS-traF control males (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical significance.

claim: Whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly higher in traF K-IN males compared with w1118 control males.
source: As in da-GAL4>UAS-traF males, whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly higher in traF K-IN males compared with w1118 control males (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The presence of rudimentary ovaries in traF K-IN males did not explain their increased fat storage.
source: Importantly, the presence of rudimentary ovaries in traF K-IN males did not explain their increased fat storage, as whole-body fat storage was still higher in traF K-IN males lacking gonads compared with gonadless control males (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F comparing gonadless males.

claim: The elevated fat storage in traF K-IN males cannot be attributed to ecdysone production by the rudimentary ovaries, as no ecdysone target genes were upregulated.
source: The elevated fat storage in traF K-IN males also cannot be attributed to ecdysone production by the rudimentary ovaries, as no ecdysone target genes were upregulated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D; Sieber and Spradling, 2015); however, future studies will need to address why these traF K-IN males showed significant ecdysone target gene downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D showing no upregulation of ecdysone target genes.

claim: Triglyceride mobilization post-starvation was significantly reduced in da-GAL4>UAS-traF males compared with da-GAL4>+ or +>UAS-traF controls during a 24-hr starvation period.
source: In males, this role for Tra may also extend to the regulation of fat breakdown, as triglyceride mobilization post-starvation was significantly reduced in da-GAL4>UAS-traF males compared with da-GAL4>+ or +>UAS-traF controls during a 24-hr starvation period (genotype:time p<0.0001 [males]; Supplementary file 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), a finding we reproduced in traF K-IN males (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E with statistical analysis.

claim: Starvation resistance was significantly reduced in tra1/Df(3L)st-j7 females compared with w1118 controls.
source: While all female genotypes lacking tra function had reduced fat storage compared with control females (Figure 5E), APC ablation in tra mutant females rescued this decrease in whole-body triglyceride levels (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Starvation resistance was significantly enhanced in da-GAL4>UAS-traF males compared with da-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-traF controls.
source: Indeed, loss of tra reduced starvation resistance in females (Figure 2A) whereas gain of Tra function enhanced starvation resistance in males (Figure 2B), in line with their effects on fat metabolism (Figure 1A and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Starvation resistance in males with Tra overexpression in neurons (elav-GAL4>UAS-traF) was significantly extended compared with elav-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-traF controls.
source: Specifically, starvation resistance in males with Tra overexpression in neurons (elav-GAL4>UAS-traF) was significantly extended compared with elav-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-traF controls (Figure 2C), with no effect in females (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly higher in elav-GAL4>UAS-traF males compared with sex-matched elav-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-traF controls.
source: We found that elav-GAL4>UAS-traF males (Figure 2D), but not females (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), showed a significant increase in whole-body fat storage compared with sex-matched elav-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-traF controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Starvation resistance was significantly enhanced in Akh-GAL4>UAS-traF males compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-traF controls.
source: Flies with APC-specific Tra expression (Akh-GAL4>UAS-traF) had significantly increased starvation resistance compared with sex-matched Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-traF controls (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There was a significant increase in whole-body fat storage in males with APC-specific Tra expression (Akh-GAL4>UAS-traF).
source: There was a significant increase in whole-body fat storage in males (Figure 2F) but not females (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B) with APC-specific Tra expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Akh mRNA levels were significantly higher in 5-day-old w1118 males than in females.
source: We first examined Akh and AkhR mRNA levels in both sexes using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR). We found that mRNA levels of both Akh and AkhR were significantly higher in 5-day-old w1118 males than in females (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A with statistical significance p<0.0001.

claim: AkhR mRNA levels were significantly higher in 5-day-old w1118 males than in females.
source: We first examined Akh and AkhR mRNA levels in both sexes using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR). We found that mRNA levels of both Akh and AkhR were significantly higher in 5-day-old w1118 males than in females (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B with statistical significance p=0.0002.

claim: There was no sex difference in the number of APCs.
source: This male bias in Akh mRNA levels did not reflect an increased APC number in males, as we found no sex difference in the number of APCs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In 5-day-old Akh-GAL4>UAS-CaLexA males, GFP levels were significantly higher than in age- and genotype-matched females.
source: In 5-day-old Akh-GAL4>UAS-CaLexA males, GFP levels were significantly higher than in age- and genotype-matched females (Figure 3D–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-H with statistical significance p=0.0438.

claim: The ratio of p-Ire1 to loading control actin was higher in 5-day-old w1118 males compared with age- and genotype-matched females in three out of four biological replicates.
source: We found that the ratio of p-Ire1 to loading control actin was higher in 5-day-old w1118 males compared with age- and genotype-matched females in three out of four biological replicates (Figure 3I–K; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), a finding that aligns with the sex difference in Akh/AkhR mRNA levels and APC activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: Triglyceride levels were significantly higher in 5-day-old Akh-GAL4>UAS-rpr males than in Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-rpr control males.
source: Triglyceride levels were significantly higher in 5-day-old Akh-GAL4>UAS-rpr males than in Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-rpr control males (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Triglyceride levels in 5-day-old Akh-GAL4>UAS-rpr females were not significantly different from Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-rpr control females.
source: In contrast, triglyceride levels in 5-day-old Akh-GAL4>UAS-rpr females were not significantly different from Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-rpr control females (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly higher in AkhA males compared with w1118 controls.
source: Importantly, we reproduced the male-biased effects on fat storage in flies carrying loss-of-function Akh and AkhR alleles (AkhA and AkhR1, respectively) (Figure 4B and C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C), and show that APC-specific knockdown of Lst had no effect on fat storage in either sex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly higher in AkhR1 males compared with AkhRrev controls.
source: Importantly, we reproduced the male-biased effects on fat storage in flies carrying loss-of-function Akh and AkhR alleles (AkhA and AkhR1, respectively) (Figure 4B and C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C), and show that APC-specific knockdown of Lst had no effect on fat storage in either sex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: APC-specific knockdown of Lst had no effect on fat storage in either sex.
source: Importantly, we reproduced the male-biased effects on fat storage in flies carrying loss-of-function Akh and AkhR alleles (AkhA and AkhR1, respectively) (Figure 4B and C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C), and show that APC-specific knockdown of Lst had no effect on fat storage in either sex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Whole-body fat storage in Akh-GAL4>UAS-Akh-RNAi adult males was significantly higher compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-Akh-RNAi control males.
source: In males, whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly higher in Akh-GAL4>UAS-Akh-RNAi flies compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-Akh-RNAi control flies (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Akh-GAL4>UAS-Akh-RNAi female flies showed no significant change in whole-body fat storage compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-Akh-RNAi control females.
source: Akh-GAL4>UAS-Akh-RNAi female flies, in contrast, showed no significant change in whole-body fat storage compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-Akh-RNAi control females (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Whole-body fat storage in Akh-GAL4>UAS-Kir2.1 adult males was significantly higher compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-Kir2.1 control males.
source: Whole-body fat storage in Akh-GAL4>UAS-Kir2.1 adult males was significantly higher compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-Kir2.1 control males (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Augmenting APC activity in females using a bacterial voltage-gated sodium channel (UAS-NaChBac) significantly reduced fat storage in females.
source: Indeed, augmenting APC activity in females using a bacterial voltage-gated sodium channel (UAS-NaChBac) significantly reduced fat storage in females (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: No significant effects of altered APC activity on feeding behavior were observed in either sex.
source: While Akh affects food-related behaviors in some contexts (Choi et al., 2015; Hentze et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2020), we observed no significant effects of altered APC activity on feeding behavior in either sex (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-D.

claim: In 5-day-old tra1/Df(3L)st-j7 females, levels of p-Ire1 were higher than in w1118 control females in three out of four biological replicates.
source: In 5-day-old tra1/Df(3L)st-j7 females, levels of p-Ire1 were higher than in w1118 control females in three out of four biological replicates (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Loss of Tra significantly increased Akh mRNA levels in females.
source: Indeed, loss of Tra significantly increased Akh mRNA levels in females (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D with statistical significance p<0.0001.

claim: APC ablation in tra mutant females rescued the decrease in whole-body triglyceride levels.
source: While all female genotypes lacking tra function had reduced fat storage compared with control females (Figure 5E), APC ablation in tra mutant females rescued this decrease in whole-body triglyceride levels (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Fat storage in tra mutant females lacking APCs was not significantly different from w1118 control females.
source: Indeed, fat storage in tra mutant females lacking APCs was not significantly different from w1118 control females (p=0.9384; Supplementary file 1; Figure 5E), indicating that the increased Akh pathway activity we observed in tra mutant females was one reason for their reduced fat storage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E with statistical analysis.

claim: APC activation in males expressing physiological levels of Tra rescued the Tra-induced increase in whole-body triglyceride levels.
source: Given that APC activation in males expressing physiological levels of Tra similarly rescued the Tra-induced increase in whole-body triglyceride levels (Figure 5F), these findings suggest that the sex-specific regulation of Akh pathway activity represents one way tra influences the male-female difference in fat storage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The proportion of AkhA males copulating with a Canton-S (CS) virgin female was lower than in control w1118 males at each 10 min interval during a 60-min observation period.
source: In AkhA mutant males, we found that the proportion of males copulating with a Canton-S (CS) virgin female was lower than in control w1118 males at each 10 min interval during a 60-min observation period (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: AkhA mutant males had significantly fewer overall progeny than w1118 control males from a 60-min mating period.
source: When we counted viable offspring from these copulation events, we found that AkhA mutant males had significantly fewer overall progeny than w1118 control males (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B with statistical significance p=0.0003.

claim: A prolonged 24 hr period of contact between AkhA mutant males and CS females allowed the production of normal progeny numbers.
source: These results suggest that Akh function normally promotes reproductive success in males; however, it is important to note that Akh function is not absolutely required for male fertility, as a prolonged 24 hr period of contact between AkhA mutant males and CS females allowed the production of normal progeny numbers (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: AkhA mutant females produced a significantly higher number of offspring compared with w1118 controls.
source: Specifically, AkhA mutant females produced a significantly higher number of offspring compared with w1118 controls (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D with statistical significance p=0.0006.

claim: Lifespan was significantly shorter in Akh-GAL4>UAS-Kir2.1 females compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-Kir2.1 control females.
source: We found that lifespan was significantly shorter in Akh-GAL4>UAS-Kir2.1 females compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-Kir2.1 control females (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Male lifespan was not significantly different between Akh-GAL4>UAS-Kir2.1 flies and Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-Kir2.1 controls.
source: In contrast, male lifespan was not significantly different between Akh-GAL4>UAS-Kir2.1 flies and Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-Kir2.1 controls (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The main form of stored fat is triglyceride, which is deposited within specialized organelles called lipid droplets.
source: The main form of stored fat is triglyceride, which is deposited within specialized organelles called lipid droplets (Kühnlein, 2012; Murphy, 2001; Thiele and Spandl, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies establishing this as scientific knowledge.

claim: The main organ responsible for triglyceride storage is the adipose tissue.
source: Lipid droplets are found in many cell types throughout the body, but the main organ responsible for triglyceride storage is the adipose tissue (Murphy, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study establishing this as scientific knowledge.

claim: The Adipokinetic hormone (Akh) pathway plays a central role in regulating whole-body fat storage and breakdown.
source: While many pathways impact whole-body triglyceride levels (Ballard et al., 2010; Bjedov et al., 2010; Broughton et al., 2005; Choi et al., 2015; DiAngelo and Birnbaum, 2009; Francis et al., 2010; Ghosh and O'Connor, 2014; Grönke et al., 2010; Heier and Kühnlein, 2018; Heier et al., 2021; Hentze et al., 2015; Kamareddine et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2017; Kubrak et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2019; Lehmann, 2018; Luong et al., 2006; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012; Roth et al., 2018; Scopelliti et al., 2019; Sieber and Spradling, 2015; Song et al., 2014; Song et al., 2017; Suzawa et al., 2019; Teleman et al., 2005; Texada et al., 2019), the Adipokinetic hormone (Akh; FBgn0004552) pathway plays a central role in regulating whole-body fat storage and breakdown (Heier and Kühnlein, 2018; Heier et al., 2021; Lehmann, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Akh is synthesized as a preprohormone in the Akh-producing cells (APCs), and is subsequently cleaved by proprotein convertases to produce active Akh.
source: Akh is synthesized as a preprohormone in the Akh-producing cells (APCs), and is subsequently cleaved by proprotein convertases to produce active Akh (Lee and Park, 2004; Noyes et al., 1995; Predel et al., 2004; Wegener et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When the APCs are activated by stimuli such as peptide hormones or neurons that make physical connections with the APCs, Akh is released into the hemolymph.
source: When the APCs are activated by stimuli such as peptide hormones or neurons that make physical connections with the APCs (Kubrak et al., 2020; Oh et al., 2019; Scopelliti et al., 2019; Zhao and Karpac, 2017), Akh is released into the hemolymph (Braco et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Circulating Akh interacts with a G-protein coupled receptor called the Akh receptor (AkhR), where Akh binding to AkhR on target tissues such as the fat body increases intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels.
source: Circulating Akh then interacts with a G-protein coupled receptor called the Akh receptor (AkhR, FBgn0025595), where Akh binding to AkhR on target tissues such as the fat body increases intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of Akh signaling pathways.

claim: High levels of cAMP activate protein kinase A (PKA).
source: High levels of cAMP activate protein kinase A (PKA; FBgg0000242) (Gäde and Auerswald, 2003; Park et al., 2002; Staubli et al., 2002), which phosphorylates several downstream metabolic effectors to promote fat breakdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In insects, active PKA promotes fat breakdown via phosphorylation and activation of Lipid storage droplet-1 (Lsd-1).
source: For example, in insects, active PKA promotes fat breakdown via phosphorylation and activation of Lipid storage droplet-1 (Lsd-1; FBgn0039114) (Arrese et al., 2008; Bickel et al., 2009; Gäde and Auerswald, 2003; Patel et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of Akh or AkhR augments fat storage in males under normal physiological conditions.
source: Indeed, loss of Akh or AkhR augments fat storage in males under normal physiological conditions (Bharucha et al., 2008; Gáliková et al., 2015; Grönke et al., 2007), highlighting the critical role of this pathway in regulating whole-body triglyceride levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Flies carrying loss-of-function mutations in genes involved in triglyceride synthesis and storage show reduced whole-body triglyceride levels.
source: For example, flies carrying loss-of-function mutations in genes involved in triglyceride synthesis and storage, such as midway (mdy; FBgn0004797), Lipin (Lpin; FBgn0263593), Lipid storage droplet-2 (Lsd-2; FBgn0030608), and Seipin (Seipin; FBgn0040336) show reduced whole-body triglyceride levels (Buszczak et al., 2002; Grönke et al., 2003; Teixeira et al., 2003; Tian et al., 2011; Ugrankar et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Whole-body deficiency for genes that regulate triglyceride breakdown generally results in higher whole-body fat levels.
source: Whole-body deficiency for genes that regulate triglyceride breakdown, on the other hand, generally have higher whole-body fat levels. This is best illustrated by elevated whole-body triglyceride levels found in flies lacking brummer (bmm; FBgn0036449) or Hsl (FBgn0034491), both of which encode lipases (Bi et al., 2012; Grönke et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Higher circulating levels of steroid hormone ecdysone in mated females promote increased whole-body fat storage.
source: In one study, higher circulating levels of steroid hormone ecdysone in mated females were found to promote increased whole-body fat storage (Sieber and Spradling, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Elevated levels of bmm mRNA in male flies restrict triglyceride storage to limit whole-body fat storage.
source: Another study showed that elevated levels of bmm mRNA in male flies restricted triglyceride storage to limit whole-body fat storage (Wat et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Neither ecdysone signaling nor bmm fully explain known male-female differences in whole-body fat metabolism.
source: Yet, neither ecdysone signaling nor bmm fully explain known male-female differences in whole-body fat metabolism (Sieber and Spradling, 2015; Wat et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In Drosophila, sexual development is determined by the number of X chromosomes.
source: In Drosophila, sexual development is determined by the number of X chromosomes (Salz and Erickson, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study establishing this as scientific knowledge.

claim: In females, the presence of two X chromosomes triggers the production of a functional splicing factor called Sex-lethal (Sxl).
source: In females, the presence of two X chromosomes triggers the production of a functional splicing factor called Sex-lethal (Sxl; FBgn0264270) (Bell et al., 1988; Bridges, 1921; Cline, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies establishing this as scientific knowledge.

claim: Sxl-dependent splicing of tra pre-mRNA allows the production of a functional Tra protein.
source: Sxl's most well-known downstream target is transformer (tra; FBgn0003741), where Sxl-dependent splicing of tra pre-mRNA allows the production of a functional Tra protein (Belote et al., 1989; Boggs et al., 1987; Inoue et al., 1990; Sosnowski et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies establishing this as scientific knowledge.

claim: In males, which have only one X chromosome, no functional Sxl or Tra proteins are made.
source: In males, which have only one X chromosome, no functional Sxl or Tra proteins are made (Cline and Meyer, 1996; Salz and Erickson, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies establishing this as scientific knowledge.

claim: Sxl and Tra direct most aspects of female sexual identity, including effects on abdominal pigmentation, egg-laying, neural circuits, and behavior.
source: Over several decades, a large body of evidence has accumulated showing that Sxl and Tra direct most aspects of female sexual identity, including effects on abdominal pigmentation, egg-laying, neural circuits, and behavior (Anand et al., 2001; Baker et al., 2001; Billeter et al., 2006; Brown and King, 1961; Burtis and Baker, 1989; Camara et al., 2008; Christiansen et al., 2002; Cline, 1978; Cline and Meyer, 1996; Clough et al., 2014; Dauwalder, 2011; Demir and Dickson, 2005; Goodwin et al., 2000; Hall, 1994; Heinrichs et al., 1998; Hoshijima et al., 1991; Inoue et al., 1992; Ito et al., 1996; Nagoshi et al., 1988; Neville et al., 2014; Nojima et al., 2014; Pavlou et al., 2016; von Philipsborn et al., 2014; Pomatto et al., 2017; Rezával et al., 2014; Rezával et al., 2016; Rideout et al., 2007; Rideout et al., 2010; Ryner et al., 1996; Sturtevant, 1945).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies have extended knowledge of how Sxl and Tra regulate additional aspects of development and physiology such as body size and intestinal stem cell proliferation.
source: More recently, studies have extended our knowledge of how Sxl and Tra regulate additional aspects of development and physiology such as body size and intestinal stem cell proliferation (Ahmed et al., 2020; Hudry et al., 2016; Millington and Rideout, 2018; Millington et al., 2021; Regan et al., 2016; Rideout et al., 2015; Sawala and Gould, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Akh-mediated regulation of the male-female difference in fat storage operates in a parallel pathway to the previously described sex-specific role of triglyceride lipase bmm.
source: Notably, this Akh-mediated regulation of the male-female difference in fat storage operates in a parallel pathway to the previously described sex-specific role of triglyceride lipase bmm (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B; Wat et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B demonstrating additive effects of AkhR and bmm mutations.

claim: Whole-body triglyceride levels were further increased in AkhR1; bmm1 males compared with AkhR1 males and bmm1 males.
source: Whole-body triglyceride levels were further increased in AkhR1; bmm1 males compared with AkhR1 males and bmm1 males (p<0.0001 and p<0.0001, respectively; one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Whole-body triglyceride levels were further increased in AkhR1; bmm1 females compared to AkhR1 females and bmm1 females.
source: Whole-body triglyceride levels were further increased in AkhR1; bmm1 females compared to AkhR1 females and bmm1 females (p=0.0024 and p<0.0001, respectively; one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Akh mRNA levels in the head and anterior half of the thorax were significantly lower in Akh-GAL4>UAS-Akh-RNAi males compared with Akh-GAL4>+ controls.
source: Akh mRNA levels in the head and anterior half of the thorax were significantly lower in Akh-GAL4>UAS-Akh-RNAi males compared with Akh-GAL4>+ controls (p=0.0008; Student's t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Akh mRNA levels in the head and anterior half of the thorax were significantly lower in Akh-GAL4>UAS-Akh-RNAi females compared with Akh-GAL4>+ controls.
source: Akh mRNA levels in the head and anterior half of the thorax were significantly lower in Akh-GAL4>UAS-Akh-RNAi females compared with Akh-GAL4>+ controls (p<0.0001; Student's t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The magnitude of the increase in fat storage upon APC silencing was larger in males than in females.
source: In females, while we observed significantly elevated whole-body fat storage in Akh-GAL4>UAS-Kir2.1 adults compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-Kir2.1 controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D), the magnitude of this increase was larger in males (sex:genotype interaction p=0.0455; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing a significant sex:genotype interaction.

claim: Whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly lower in Akh-GAL4>UAS-NaChBac males compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-NaChBac controls.
source: Whole-body triglyceride levels were significantly lower in Akh-GAL4>UAS-NaChBac males compared with Akh-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-NaChBac controls (p<0.0001 and p<0.0001, respectively; one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Whole-body triglyceride levels in traF K-IN males with APC activation (Akh-GAL4>UAS-NaChBac) were significantly lower than traF K-IN males carrying either the Akh-GAL4>+ or +>UAS-NaChBac transgenes alone.
source: Whole-body triglyceride levels in traF K-IN males with APC activation (Akh-GAL4>UAS-NaChBac) were significantly lower than traF K-IN males carrying either the Akh-GAL4>+ or +>UAS-NaChBac transgenes alone (p<0.0001 and p<0.0001, respectively; one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Akh function is not absolutely required for male fertility.
source: These results suggest that Akh function normally promotes reproductive success in males; however, it is important to note that Akh function is not absolutely required for male fertility, as a prolonged 24 hr period of contact between AkhA mutant males and CS females allowed the production of normal progeny numbers (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C showing no significant difference in progeny number after 24 hr mating.

claim: In females, a low level of Akh pathway activity promotes fecundity.
source: Thus, in females, a low level of Akh pathway activity promotes fecundity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that AkhA mutant females (which have no Akh pathway activity) have increased fecundity.

claim: While low Akh activity in females promotes fertility, this benefit comes at the cost of a shorter lifespan.
source: This suggests that while low Akh activity in females promotes fertility, this benefit comes at the cost of a shorter lifespan, a possibility that will be explored in future studies using additional strains to genetically augment, or inhibit, Akh pathway activity (e.g., APC activation, Akh mutants).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing increased fecundity but decreased lifespan in females with reduced Akh pathway activity.

claim: The sex-specific regulation of Akh pathway activity represents one way tra influences the male-female difference in fat storage.
source: Given that APC activation in males expressing physiological levels of Tra similarly rescued the Tra-induced increase in whole-body triglyceride levels (Figure 5F), these findings suggest that the sex-specific regulation of Akh pathway activity represents one way tra influences the male-female difference in fat storage.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic rescue experiments showing that manipulating Akh pathway activity can rescue Tra-dependent effects on fat storage.

claim: The male bias in Akh pathway activity contributes to the sex difference in fat storage by limiting whole-body triglyceride storage in males.
source: Genetic manipulation of APCs and Akh pathway activity suggest a model in which the sex bias in Akh pathway activity contributes to the male-female difference in fat storage by limiting whole-body triglyceride storage in males (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing male-biased effects of Akh pathway manipulation on fat storage.

claim: Akh acts genetically downstream of Tra in regulating whole-body triglyceride levels.
source: Importantly, we show that Tra function influences Akh pathway activity, and that Akh acts genetically downstream of Tra in regulating whole-body triglyceride levels (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is based on genetic epistasis experiments showing that manipulating Akh pathway activity can rescue Tra-dependent effects on fat storage.

claim: The presence of Tra in females normally represses Akh pathway activity.
source: This suggests the presence of Tra in females normally represses Akh pathway activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that loss of Tra in females increases Akh pathway activity.

claim: The increased Akh pathway activity observed in tra mutant females was one reason for their reduced fat storage.
source: Indeed, fat storage in tra mutant females lacking APCs was not significantly different from w1118 control females (p=0.9384; Supplementary file 1; Figure 5E), indicating that the increased Akh pathway activity we observed in tra mutant females was one reason for their reduced fat storage.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic rescue experiment showing that removing APCs in tra mutant females rescues their fat storage phenotype.

claim: The male-specific increase in starvation resistance in elav-GAL4>UAS-traF males was due to increased fat storage.
source: This suggests that the male-specific increase in starvation resistance (Figure 2C) was due to increased fat storage in elav-GAL4>UAS-traF males, which we confirm by showing that the rate of fat breakdown in elav-GAL4>UAS-traF males and females was not significantly different from sex-matched elav-GAL4>+ and +>UAS-traF controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C) (genotype:time interaction p=0.2789 [males], p=0.7058 [females]; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing increased fat storage but no change in fat breakdown in elav-GAL4>UAS-traF males.

claim: Tra function in the APCs promotes fat storage.
source: This indicates Tra function in the APCs promotes fat storage, revealing a previously unrecognized role for the APCs in regulating the sex difference in fat storage.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that APC-specific Tra expression increases fat storage in males.

claim: The male bias in Akh pathway activity normally contributes to the sex difference in fat storage by limiting triglyceride accumulation in males via the established intracellular signaling cascade known to regulate lipid droplet breakdown.
source: This suggests that the male bias in Akh pathway activity normally contributes to the sex difference in fat storage by limiting triglyceride accumulation in males via the established intracellular signaling cascade known to regulate lipid droplet breakdown (Arrese et al., 2008; Heier and Kühnlein, 2018; Heier et al., 2021; Kühnlein, 2012; Patel et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing male-biased effects of APC ablation on fat storage, combined with established knowledge of Akh signaling.

claim: It is Akh production by the APCs that plays a role in regulating the male-female difference in fat storage.
source: Importantly, we reproduced the male-biased effects on fat storage in flies carrying loss-of-function Akh and AkhR alleles (AkhA and AkhR1, respectively) (Figure 4B and C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C), and show that APC-specific knockdown of Lst had no effect on fat storage in either sex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E). These findings support a model in which it is Akh production by the APCs that plays a role in regulating the male-female difference in fat storage.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that Akh and AkhR mutants have male-biased effects on fat storage, while Lst knockdown does not.

claim: The sex difference in Akh mRNA levels contributes to the male-female difference in whole-body fat storage.
source: This indicates a strongly male-biased effect on fat storage due to reduced Akh mRNA levels, suggesting that the sex difference in Akh mRNA levels contributes to the male-female difference in whole-body fat storage.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that reducing Akh mRNA levels has male-biased effects on fat storage.

claim: The male bias in APC activity contributes to the sex difference in fat storage by limiting triglyceride accumulation in males.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the male bias in APC activity contributes to the sex difference in fat storage by limiting triglyceride accumulation in males.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that silencing APCs has larger effects on fat storage in males than in females.

claim: The male-biased effect of APC manipulation on fat storage cannot be fully explained by effects on food intake.
source: While Akh affects food-related behaviors in some contexts (Choi et al., 2015; Hentze et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2020), we observed no significant effects of altered APC activity on feeding behavior in either sex (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-D). This suggests that the male-biased effect of APC manipulation on fat storage cannot be fully explained by effects on food intake.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing no significant effects on food intake despite effects on fat storage.

claim: GAL4 mRNA levels were not significantly different between males and females carrying the Akh-GAL4 transgene.
source: Because GAL4 mRNA levels were not significantly different between males and females carrying the Akh-GAL4 transgene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and the number of APCs did not differ between the sexes (Figure 3C), these findings indicate that the APCs are more active in males than in females.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The APCs are more active in males than in females.
source: Because GAL4 mRNA levels were not significantly different between males and females carrying the Akh-GAL4 transgene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and the number of APCs did not differ between the sexes (Figure 3C), these findings indicate that the APCs are more active in males than in females.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing higher GFP intensity in male APCs using the CaLexA system, combined with evidence that GAL4 levels and APC number do not differ between sexes.

claim: High levels of Akh pathway activity limit fat storage whereas low levels of Akh signaling promote fat storage.
source: Thus, high levels of Akh pathway activity limit fat storage whereas low levels of Akh signaling promote fat storage.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of Akh pathway function.

claim: Loss of Akh or AkhR augments fat storage in males under normal physiological conditions, highlighting the critical role of this pathway in regulating whole-body triglyceride levels.
source: Indeed, loss of Akh or AkhR augments fat storage in males under normal physiological conditions (Bharucha et al., 2008; Gáliková et al., 2015; Grönke et al., 2007), highlighting the critical role of this pathway in regulating whole-body triglyceride levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claim: Levels of phosphorylated Ire1 (p-Ire1) are higher in Drosophila cells stimulated with Akh peptide, regulation that was dependent on the presence of AkhR.
source: Because levels of phosphorylated Ire1 (p-Ire1) are higher in Drosophila cells stimulated with Akh peptide, regulation that was dependent on the presence of AkhR, high p-Ire1 levels indicate increased Akh pathway activity (Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: High p-Ire1 levels indicate increased Akh pathway activity.
source: Because levels of phosphorylated Ire1 (p-Ire1) are higher in Drosophila cells stimulated with Akh peptide, regulation that was dependent on the presence of AkhR, high p-Ire1 levels indicate increased Akh pathway activity (Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from a previous study showing that p-Ire1 levels correlate with Akh pathway activity.
